items.title: Single-Family Permitting Weakens While Multifamily Activity Remains Stronger
items.description: Single-Family Permitting Weakens While Multifamily Activity Remains Stronger November 16, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Residential permitting activity continued to show divergent trends across the single-family and multifamily sectors through September 2026. Single-family permitting remained under pressure, with year-to-date activity declining from a year earlier amid ongoing housing affordability challenges and elevated construction costs. In contrast, multifamily permitting recorded growth, reflecting stronger activity in several regions and states. Over the first nine months of the year, the number of single-family permits issued nationwide reached 689,884. Compared with the same period in 2025, this represents a 3.0% decline from the September 2025 total of 711,020. In contrast, multifamily permitting activity remained stronger, with 393,778 permits issued nationwide, marking a 4.1% increase compared with the same period last year. Regionally, year-to-date single-family permitting declined in three out of the four regions through September. The Midwest was the only region to post an increase, with single-family permits rising 0.6%. The South declined 1.9%, the West fell 5.7%, and the Northeast posted the largest decline at 11.8%. Multifamily permits increased in three of the four regions, led by the Northeast (28.2%), followed by the West (9.7%), and the Midwest (5.3%). The South was the only region to post a decline, with multifamily permits falling 5.8%, driven largely by reduced permitting activity in major metropolitan areas across the region. At the state level, 19 states and the District of Columbia recorded increases in single-family permits compared with the same period last year, with gains ranging from 45.5% in the District of Columbia to 0.5% in Wisconsin. The remaining 31 states posted declines. Nevada recorded the steepest decline, with single-family permits falling 25.2%. The ten states issued the highest number of single-family permits accounted for 62.2% of all single-family permits issued nationwide. Texas led the nation with 108,433 permits issued through September 2026, although this represented a 3.1% decline from the same period in 2025. Florida, the second-highest state, recorded a 0.6% decline, while North Carolina, ranking third, posted a 7.9% decrease. Through September, 29 states and the District of Columbia recorded increases in multifamily building permits, while 21 states experienced declines. Kansas posted the largest percentage increase, with multifamily permits rising 99.6%, from 3,041 to 6,071 units. In contrast, Vermont recorded the steepest decline, with permits falling 72.1%, from 982 to 274 units. The ten states issued the highest number of multifamily permits accounted for 60.8% of all multifamily permits issued nationwide. Through the first nine months of 2026, Texas, which issued the largest number of multifamily permits, posted a 17.9% decline compared with the same period last year. California, the second-highest state, recorded a 23.2% increase, while Florida, ranking third, saw multifamily permits decrease by 24.2%. items.title: Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales
items.description: Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses. In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap. Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets. Discount to home values at center of dispute Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire. The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home. “REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter. Years of underperformance versus peers Land & Buildings also highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter said. Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb. The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter. Capital allocation and legal settlements under scrutiny Land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm said. The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm. “This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said. Call for $2 billion a year in capital returns The activist laid out a three-part plan it says could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value: Commit to at least $2 billion a year in capital returns. Land & Buildings wants Invitation Homes to pledge to return a minimum of $2 billion annually to shareholders on a leverage-neutral basis, funded by selling homes individually into the for-sale market. Capital could be returned through share repurchases or special dividends for as long as the stock trades below estimated NAV. Offer renters a path to homeownership. The plan calls for providing existing tenants a 6% rebate to cover a down payment if they buy the home they rent. Land & Buildings argues that rebate roughly matches the brokerage, repair and vacancy costs of an open-market sale, allowing the company to expand homeownership opportunities “for thousands of renters at little or no incremental cost.” Scale back acquisitions and development. The firm recommended Invitation Homes “significantly curtail external growth activities” while its cost of capital is elevated, saying there is “no better use of the Company’s capital than its own stock.” Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value. items.title: Where Developers Are Trying To Lease Public Lands To Build Data Centers
items.description: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Flickr/Bureau of Land Management The Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area in Idaho, where the Bureau of Land Management is considering leasing a parcel of public land for a data center development Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks . The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act . Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws . This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow ’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Flickr/U.S. Department of Energy Excavation of the Portsmouth site in 2012 as part of soil remediation efforts at the former uranium enrichment plant Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September . BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. items.title: Service Properties Trust Rejects $2B Cash Bid, Claims Hotel Portfolio Could Be Worth Double
items.description: Service Properties Trust rejected a $2B offer for its hotel portfolio that would have accelerated its plans to transition to a pure-play triple-net lease REIT. Google Maps The Royal Sonesta New Orleans, owned by Service Properties Trust The board, including all six independent trustees, unanimously agreed that offloading the portfolio would not be in the best interests of its shareholders, according to a letter published Friday. Jim Koehler’s TKO made an unsolicited offer for 93 of the REIT’s assets on Oct. 7. The $2B all-cash bid exceeds SVC's entire market capitalization of less than $1B. Rather than taking the offer, the company plans to retain its 77 hotels before selling them starting next year. Service Properties Trust, which is managed by The RMR Group and trades under the ticker SVC, expects that the hotels will grow earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization by approximately $109M within 12 to 24 months, according to the letter. Doing so will allow the REIT to achieve higher sales prices, the board argued. SVC began selling assets in 2025 to pay down debts. In the third quarter, the company reported a net loss of $87.9M , down further from a $46.9M loss during the same period last year. Its funds from operations, a core measure of cash flow for REITs, were $0.31 per share, down from $0.92 a year prior. This year, SVC said it completed 14 of the 15 planned hotel sales for $116.7M combined. It is marketing two more hotels, according to its third-quarter investor presentation. TKO followed up on its offer on Oct. 15 , stating that the investment firm “is prepared to deliver proof of funds demonstrating its strong financial capacity and wherewithal to complete the proposed transaction.” It offered to deposit $50M into escrow to demonstrate its commitment. “Despite submitting an all cash offer, TKO contends that it has received no meaningful response from SVC,” the company said in the statement. “TKO maintains that this silence is difficult to reconcile with SVC's public statements regarding its intention to sell its hotel assets.” SVC originally revealed its rejection in an investor presentation on Nov. 5 , claiming that the $2B offer significantly undervalues the portfolio. Activist Blackwells Capital challenged the decision in a letter published a day later. It argued that RMR's financial ties to hotel operator Sonesta International Hotels create conflicts of interest and that a sale could trigger substantial management termination or transition payments, potentially giving RMR an incentive to resist a deal. The letter, penned by Blackwells Chief Investment Officer Jason Aintabi, highlighted that SVC’s share price is down 85% in five years and 35% in a year. “A board that tells its owners the hotels alone are worth significantly more than $2.0 billion has exactly one legitimate way to prove it: a genuine process, run in the open, by unconflicted trustees," Aintabi said in a statement released alongside the letter. Adjusted hotel EBITDA for SVC’s 77 retained hotels was $41.1M in the third quarter, a 16% increase year-over-year. The REIT said it has invested $628M in those assets since 2023, which has driven an 8% increase in revenue per available room. In its Friday letter responding to Blackwells, the board claimed that the results illustrate that the hotels could be worth between $3B and $4.1B in aggregate. “The Board believes that allowing this growth to take hold before selling offers the opportunity to realize significantly higher proceeds for shareholders than selling the hotels today,” the board wrote. In the last five days, SVC's stock price climbed more than 13%, including 2% between market open and noon on Monday. SVC plans to begin selling the properties individually or in small portfolios and expects to offload all of the properties by the end of 2028. “The Board would seriously consider credible proposals for the Retained Hotels that would accelerate SVC’s transition to a de-levered pure play triple net lease REIT, provided that, in the Board’s judgment, they appropriately value the Retained Hotels and are in the best interests of SVC and all its shareholders,” the board wrote. “TKO’s proposal simply did not meet these standards.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Blackwells Capital , Jason Aintabi , Net Lease , Service Properties Trust , Sonesta International Hotels , The RMR Group , TKO , Triple Net Lease

items.title: Who Owns Outright? Mortgage Status, Lock-In and Senior Homeownership
items.description: Who Owns Outright? Mortgage Status, Lock-In and Senior Homeownership By Jiayi Xu Nov 16, 2026 Tax Bill Survey Highlights The share of owner-occupied homes owned outright continues to grow. In 2025, 41% of owner-occupied homes were owned free and clear, and 59% still carried a mortgage. Mortgage shares fell across all four regions. The West has the highest share of homes with a mortgage, and the South has the lowest. At the state level, the District of Columbia has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.5%), and West Virginia has the lowest (43.4%). Among the 50 largest metros, Washington, DC has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.6%), and Miami has the lowest (54.1%). More households aged 75+ own their homes, and more owners carry a mortgage Homeownership among households aged 75+ rose to 78.3% in 2025, up from 75.7% in 2010. The mortgage-free share among owners aged 75+ fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. Most still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%. Among the 50 largest metros, mortgages are least common among owners aged 75+ in Grand Rapids, MI, and most common in Riverside, CA. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of the generational housing handoff. Owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. Mortgage rates have been a central constraint on the housing market, and rate changes affect markets differently depending not only on how the mortgage rates that current homeowners pay differ from the market , but also on how much of the housing stock is financed. Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs. Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs. With mortgage rates back above 7% and potential Federal Funds rate hikes in 2027 , the lock-in effect is likely to tighten the market again . Owners with low-rate loans are reluctant to give up their rate, which keeps homes off the market. One channel through which these effects accumulate is generational housing succession . The oldest baby boomers, born in 1946, turned 80 in 2026, and as this generation moves into its 80s, a growing number of the homes they own will be released back to the open market. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of that handoff: owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. To understand the differences in geographic impact of high mortgage rates, we use the 2025 1-Year Estimate from the American Community Survey. items.title: Blackstone's Data Center REIT Makes First Investment With $5B AWS Deal
items.description: Blackstone ’s recently listed data center acquisition business made its first purchase, a $5B stake in Amazon -leased data centers. Unsplash/Scott Rodgerson Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust is acquiring a 75% majority stake in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services to acquire 13 newly constructed powered shells across two AWS campuses in a deal valued at $5B, the investment management giant announced Monday . Amazon will lease back 100% of the portfolio from the REIT, which trades under the ticker BXDC, on a triple-net basis with an initial term of 12 years and an option to expand the length to 32 years. Rent payments are guaranteed by AWS, according to a presentation published with the announcement. The inaugural acquisition for the REIT comes at a 7.0% capitalization rate. Two-thirds of the portfolio is in the greater Chicago region with the remainder in Mississippi. “The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds,” BXDC CEO Nick Pell said in a statement. “Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders.” The transaction is expected to close before the end of the year. Blackstone launched the public REIT in May . The business is seeking newly constructed but stabilized data centers occupied by “top investment-grade hyperscalers ” valued between $250B and $1.5B. BXDC is targeting returns between 5.75% and 7% or more, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission . Blackstone has been one of the most active backers of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers and power facilities through its Blackstone Energy Transition Partners. It was early to the data center race, agreeing in 2021 to acquire QTS Realty Trust at a $10B valuation . The investment giant’s flagship private real estate fund, Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust , deployed $3.4B into preleased data center development through QTS in the third quarter, bringing its year-to-date deployment to the sector to roughly $9B. Shares in BXDC were up more than 7% in premarket trading following the announcement of the deal with AWS but gave up some of those gains at the opening bell. items.title: Lenders increasingly pull with new credit score model, but few use it for pricing
items.description: Mortgage lenders are frequently pulling credit scores with VantageScore 4.0, but most of them still price with Classic FICO , according to a new Bank of America Global Research report based on Recursion data. The report, released on Friday, shows that Rocket Mortgage and United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) are driving nearly all of the production actually priced with the new scoring model in the agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) market. Since October, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have required that agency MBS pools disclose both Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0 whenever both are pulled, and to identify which score was used for pricing. According to Bank of America, 148 sellers in October delivered agency MBS loans for which a VS4 score had been pulled. That figure rose to 173 sellers during the first 10 days of November. But the number of lenders actually pricing loans with VS4 remains much smaller. Only eight lenders sold loans priced with VS4 in September, which rose to 22 in October and 37 to date in November. In October, 20% of conventional issuance reported a VS4 score, BofA said. Of that subset, 39% used VS4 as the pricing score, which works out to roughly 8% of total conventional issuance. Most of these loans had both scores: 18% of issuance reported both FICO and VS4 , while only 2% reported VS4 alone. Thus far in November, 21% of issuance had VS4 reported and 32% of these loans used VS4 for pricing, or about 7% of total issuance. Early adopters Rocket and UWM are the main early adopters on the pricing side. In October, BofA found that Rocket and UWM together accounted for 65% of all loans with a VS4 score pulled. They also were the sources for 95% of loans that used VS4 as their pricing score in the agency MBS market. Among other lenders that have shown they can pull VS4, just 13% of their production had a VS4 score reported and only 1% of loans actually used VS4 to set prices. “We think this disconnect largely reflects a gradual ramp-up in operational and infrastructure readiness,” BofA analysts said. “Pulling and reporting an additional score is relatively straightforward, while actually incorporating VS4 into loan pricing likely requires more extensive changes to lenders' pricing systems and operational infrastructure.” BofA’s report also notes that loans priced with VS4 have distinctive collateral characteristics. VS4-priced loans tend to have higher average loan balances , a lower share of first-time homebuyers , and higher shares of cash-out and rate-and-term refinance loans. Among VS4-priced loans where both scores were reported, the VS4 score was on average about 43 points higher than FICO. For FICO-priced loans with both scores present, the two models are broadly comparable, the analysts said. Because lenders can choose between scores when both are present, the emerging “best-of-two” selection framework is affecting the distribution of published scores. BofA found that among October loans with both scores reported, 24% had FICO scores below 700 and 21% had VS4 scores below 700, but only 17% had a pricing score below 700. Potential refis BofA also addressed investor concerns that borrowers in legacy low-FICO pools who have materially higher VS4 scores could see a one-time chance to refinance as markets and pricing grids adjust to VS4. “We acknowledge that legacy low-FICO pools are exposed to this risk,” the analysts said. “However, newly issued low credit score pools may offer a way to mitigate this risk and potentially access even better convexity collateral.” According to the report, low credit score pool collateral today generally consists of loans that either have both FICO and VS4 reported with both scores below 700, or are VS4-only loans. Loans with both FICO and VS4 below 700 have already been screened against the risk that a significantly higher VS4 score would give borrowers a one-time refinancing opportunity. Additionally, a historical analysis indicates that loans with both scores below 700 exhibit better convexity than loans defined only by FICOs below 700. Related More: Credit Score FICO VantageScore

items.title: Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
items.description:
Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered
      Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Phoenix-area residents

PHOENIX – November 17, 2026 – Nearly two-thirds of Phoenix-area residents have considered moving
because of housing costs, and 91% say housing affordability is a serious problem, according to a new
survey of Phoenix-area residents. Yet most are unaware that Congress recently passed federal
legislation, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built rental
homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: Over 91% of Phoenix-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 65% have considered moving because of housing costs.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 68% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   A majority of residents support new rental housing: 55% of Phoenix residents support
       building more rental homes, nearly 2-to-1 over those opposed.
   ●   Renters are feeling affordability pressures: 77% have considered moving because of housing
       costs.


“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman, CEO
of the National Rental Home Council and former Acting Secretary of the U.S. Department of Housing and
Urban Development during the Biden Administration.

The findings come as Arizona policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following federal
action this past summer. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act authorized several new programs,
streamlined existing programs, like the HOME grant program, and placed limits on large institutional
investors from purchasing existing single-family homes.

“As state policymakers look ahead to 2027,” Todman said. “the opportunity is to help families find a home
that works for them, close to the jobs and communities they’ve built their lives around.”

About the survey
The survey of 600 Phoenix-area residents was conducted by Pollfish in September 2026.

items.title: America’s Trillion-Dollar Credit Card Debt Threatens To Lock Millions Out of the Housing Market
items.description: With prices still alarmingly high, it comes as no surprise that Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards more than ever. But doing so could be silently sabotaging any hope of owning a home , if you’re not careful. Last week, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published its latest household debt report . Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier, and total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans, and student loans, expanded by $334 billion for the period to a record $19.1 trillion. High levels of debt are problematic for anyone, but most especially for first-time homebuyers. If your ambitions for 2027 include buying a home, it’s important to get your debt in check before it’s too late. Easy money comes at a price According to TransUnion’s most recent quarterly credit industry insights report , the number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million up from 174.8 million. The ease of use means most people turn to credit cards for their everyday purchases, like groceries, gas, and utility bills—all of which have seen a steep increase in prices over the past two years. Now, if you’re someone who pays off their credit card in full each month, you’re in the clear. If not, the average interest rate on a new credit card offer currently stands at about 24%, and debt can accumulate quickly. And this can cause an array of issues for first-time homebuyers. "Issues arising from high levels of consumer debt are amplified for first-time homebuyers as they typically have less savings, limited financial history, and tighter financial conditions,” John Donikian , vice president of Best Interest Financial in West Bloomfield, MI , tells Realtor.com® . Loading... Credit card debt is nothing to ignore, especially if you're hoping to buy a home. Getty Images The problem with carrying too much credit card debt Firstly, carrying too much debt can negatively affect your credit score , a vital metric in getting a mortgage. While there is no firm number to qualify for a mortgage, a good credit score ranges from 700 to 749, and most conventional loans typically require at least 620. Lenders may accept lower scores if you have a larger down payment or other strong financial factors. The higher your balances are, the more your score is dragged down, which can not only affect the interest rate a lender can offer you, but also keep you from getting a mortgage with some lenders entirely. “Your credit score doesn’t just determine if you are approved; it influences your interest rate and the monthly payment you are offered,” says Jake Vehige , president of mortgage lending at Neighbors Bank. “Even a small difference in interest rates can add up to thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.” Secondly, as part of the process of getting a mortgage, lenders will look at your debt-to-income ratio to see how much house you can afford. If a lender looks at your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income and your DTI exceeds its caps, your application could be delayed or even denied outright. But both of those instances can be reversed, with time and a fixed budget that allows you to pay off your debt. In other words, your credit score can rebound. Where first-time buyers are really at a disadvantage by accumulating so much credit card debt is the drain it will put on their savings. The money that you’ll need to rack up to pay off the 20%-plus interest on your bills could have been money saved for your down payment, closing costs, and repair funds. Many lenders also require proof of postclosing cash reserves, which is much harder to build while paying down high-interest debt. “Ideally, you want to keep your credit card balances at no more than 20% to 30% of your maximum credit limit," explains Jeremy Schachter , branch manager at Fairway Independent Mortgage Corp. in Phoenix . "For example, if you have a $1,000 limit, don’t go over a balance higher than $200 to $300. Anything that exceeds that amount can lower your credit score and make it difficult to get approved for a mortgage with a good rate.” Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. She previously served as the managing editor at HollywoodLife.com, the executive editor at PerezHilton.com, and as a managing editor at Mediavine. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

items.title: The Tuccori commission settlements were supposed to wrap up, then the judge asked for more
items.description: Many real estate industry players were hoping to head into the holiday season with homebuyer commission lawsuit claims squarely in the rearview mirror, but that is not how the expected final approval hearing for the Tuccori commission lawsuit settlements played out. At a hearing earlier this month, the court decided it needed a closer look at how the settlements and opt-in settlements came to be before issuing a final ruling. The settlements in question include those reached by the National Association of Realtors ($52.25 million), Compass ($7.33 million), eXp World Holdings ($4.34 million), Hanna Holdings ($8.25), HomeServices of America ($30 million) and Douglas Elliman ($2.04 million). Like many of the defendants that settled via the Tuccori opt-in option, these parties were originally named as defendants in the Batton 1 and 2 , Cwynar , Davis and Lutz lawsuits. In an order earlier this month, the judge created a list of things the court would like further information on before issuing its ruling on the settlements. Much of the information focuses on how the settlement amounts were determined and whether they are fair to settlement class members. Specifically, the court is seeking clarification on whether previous home seller settlements are an appropriate benchmark for the buyer settlements, given that those agreements resolved both buyer and seller claims. She also wants to understand how each settling defendant’s or opt-in’s financial ability to pay and transaction volume factored into its settlement amount, and what plaintiffs could realistically expect to recover if they continued litigating and went to trial. Additionally, the judge is asking the parties to provide examples of settlement benchmarks from other indirect purchaser class actions and to estimate how much individual claimants and class members would actually receive under the proposed settlements. The settling parties have until Dec. 14, 2026, to submit briefs addressing these five topics. After reviewing these briefs, the court said it will then consider if further responses are necessary. This outcome is certainly a blow to the suit’s numerous real estate brokerage defendants, as well as NAR. In an emailed statement a spokesperson for the NAR told HousingWire that the trade group "continues to believe the Tuccori settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the class. "The court’s ongoing review is a standard part of the settlement approval process, and we remain confident in the meaningful protections the settlement offers across the industry, including a broad release for Realtor members, Realtor associations, MLSs, and those brokerages that meet the settlement’s eligibility requirements," the spokesperson added. "NAR remains committed to fostering fair, transparent, and pro-consumer real estate markets while providing resources and value to our Realtor members nationwide.” The opt-in settlements, which total over $120 million, gained preliminary approval in late May . At this hearing, the court rejected the claims that these settlements were the result of a “ reverse auction ,” instead finding that the proposed opt-in settlements were “fair, reasonable and adequate,” and that the “Opt-In Agreements compensate indirect purchaser claims at almost the same rate as the claims previously resolved by the [home seller] Burnett , Gibson, Keel and Hooper settlements.” Related More: Commission Lawsuit NAR Lawsuit Settlement National Association of Realtors

items.title: Amid ‘economic headwinds,’ Boston looks to ease its inclusionary zoning policy
items.description: Amid ‘economic headwinds,’ Boston looks to ease its inclusionary zoning policy The city is proposing reduced developer fees and higher thresholds for affordable housing mandates. Published Nov. 16, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Boston Mayor Michelle Wu on Nov. 10, 2026, proposed a number of changes to the city's inclusionary zoning policy to encourage more development. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 2 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu last week proposed easing the city’s inclusionary zoning requirements “in the continued face of economic headwinds,” according to a news release. Proposed changes include reducing developer payment-in-lieu fees, extending affordable housing payment schedules and temporarily raising the threshold from seven units to 10 for the size of multifamily housing that must participate. “By providing greater flexibility and reducing upfront costs, we can help make more housing and commercial development financially feasible while preserving the affordability requirements that are so important to Boston’s future,” Boston Chief of Planning Kairos Shen said in a statement. Dive Insight: In a subdued housing market , more cities are adjusting affordable housing mandates for developers. San Francisco this summer slashed its affordable housing requirements for multifamily developers from 15% of units to 5%, according to Mission Local. New Orleans reduced its per-unit affordable housing fee by more than 96% — from $304,810 to $10,000, New Orleans City Business reported last month. Boston’s inclusionary zoning policies, which require 17% of qualifying multifamily units to be income-restricted, have produced nearly 3,000 affordable housing units over the past five years, according to Wu. Wu’s proposal cuts condominium payment-in-lieu fees — fees paid to the city when a developer does not include required affordable units — from 75% to 50% of the difference between market-rate and income-restricted unit values. Developers also could spread out those payments across seven installments instead of two. “This balanced approach is part of our administration’s broader strategy to build more homes, remove barriers to development, and ensure Boston remains a city where residents can afford to stay and thrive,” Wu said. The Boston Planning Department advanced the proposal Nov. 12. Now it will go before the Boston Zoning Commission and the City Council for approval. “We recognize that the cost of building housing has increased, and we want to be responsive to these realities,” Boston Chief of Housing Sheila Dillon said in a news release. “These program changes are designed to encourage the development of new housing while maintaining our commitment to affordability.” Recommended Reading These 3 housing programs are showing results. California + Orange County + Hospitality | November 16, 2026 By: Paul Bubny Waterfall Originates Loan for Disneyland Lodging Property Waterfall Asset Management, on behalf of its clients, originated a $48-million senior mortgage loan to Dynamic City Capital (DCC) to fund the refinancing of the Portofino Inn & Suites Anaheim near Disneyland. DCC will use proceeds to fund capital improvements and to pay off its existing loan. Built in 2000 and renovated in 2012, the Portofino Inn & Suites Anaheim is a 190-key upper midscale hotel. The hotel's amenities include an outdoor pool and a fitness center. Waterfall's Commercial Real Estate team, led by Zachary Liebmann, worked closely with DCC to structure and execute the financing. JLL's Hotels & Hospitality and Capital Markets Group served as the broker. "Waterfall's investment in Portofino Inn & Suites Anaheim provides our firm an exciting opportunity to access a Disneyland market that continues to see strong demand," said Doug Kosann, VP at Waterfall. "DCC's well-established presence in this market made them an ideal partner, and we are pleased to help them both refinance their debt and fund renovations." items.description: Realpage’s New York lawsuit tests the limits of algorithmic rent-pricing bans RealPage Inc. v. James “could provide meaningful guidance on how far state and local governments can go in regulating or restricting these technologies,” a lawyer told Multifamily Dive. A lawsuit regarding New York state’s algorithmic rent-setting ban is testing how far the government can go in restricting such tools without also overly impeding commercial speech, and may provide more clarity about what is within legal bounds, legal experts say. Although it’s difficult to estimate how influential the ultimate decision in RealPage Inc. v. James will be, the preliminary ruling indicates “the case could provide meaningful guidance on how far state and local governments can go in regulating or restricting these technologies without running afoul of the First Amendment,” Corinne Migliazza, associate at real estate law firm Otten Johnson, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. In 2024, the Department of Justice and several states sued Realpage and several major landlords that used its pricing product, alleging in United States et al. v. RealPage Inc. et al. that the use of algorithmic software to coordinate rents violated antitrust law. As settlements from that case started rolling out, New York became the first state, in 2025, to impose an outright ban on residential rent-pricing algorithms with its antitrust law amendment S.7882 . Before New York’s ban was set to take effect last year, Realpage went on the offensive. It sued the state in November 2025 on free speech grounds rather than making antitrust arguments. Then it asked the court to halt the ban while its case was being heard. The federal judge agreed to grant a preliminary injunction at the end of September and also denied the state’s January request to dismiss the lawsuit. Judge Valerie Caproni said that some language of the ban likely restricts protected speech more broadly than necessary because it is “undiscerning in targeting software without regard to its use of public versus non-public data.” Although the judge indicated the decision would be a close call, her ruling hints that the court is skeptical of New York’s restrictions, “at least enough to allow more evidence and fact to be developed and presented,” according to Migliazza. “There are also suggestions that the Court may be more receptive to narrowly tailored restrictions, like the initial RealPage settlements, which restricted the algorithms to publicly available information, rather than prohibiting their use outright,” Migliazza said. It remains to be seen whether the court will address particular uses of algorithmic rent-pricing tools in depth. It may decide to only rule on the constitutionality of New York’s restrictions and put the ball in the legislature’s court to find a better solution, according to Migliazza. “Certainly, a First Amendment victory by RealPage would force the legislature back to the drawing board to contour the law towards constitutionality – meaning they would have to make the restrictions less severe,” Migliazza said. New York case impact Algorithmic rent-pricing restrictions are proliferating: New Jersey’s FAIR Act is set to take effect on July 1, 2027, although it is structured differently from New York’s law. Jersey City, New Jersey; Providence, Rhode Island; Philadelphia; Minneapolis; San Francisco; Seattle; Rockville, Maryland, have also passed similar measures. That growing patchwork of algorithmic pricing laws is making compliance more complicated for the rental housing industry, Peter Carstensen, antitrust expert and professor of law emeritus at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Multifamily Dive. “What's a developer to do, especially if those regulations are in some way contrary to each other?” Carstensen said. It’s important for rental housing firms to follow these information exchange lawsuits and antitrust litigation more broadly, and to ask, “What are the red lights or the yellow lights that we need to watch out for? How do we make sure that people down in marketing are not creating problems for us?” according to Carstensen. Indeed, landlords are not necessarily in the clear to use algorithmic pricing tools, legal experts at law firm Lowenstein Sandler wrote. They urged caution in New York, and said to prepare for changes in New Jersey and varied algorithmic pricing laws more generally. “Tools that pool competitors’ nonpublic data, discourage price reductions, standardize lease terms, or otherwise limit independent decision-making should be closely reviewed,” according to Lowenstein Sandler. Consultation on the front end to ensure compliance with the relevant jurisdiction’s regulations could save a lot of time, energy and money later on, according to Migliazza, particularly as such regulations continue to evolve. “There is no doubt that as the technological landscape surrounding artificial intelligence changes, the legal one will too,” she said. The state is arguing that Realpage lacks standing to represent third parties who are not named plaintiffs and that S.7882 represents constitutional regulation of commercial speech. items.title: Craig Hall Is Betting on the Future of Office. His Next Chapter at HALL Park Is Taking Shape.
items.description: Live Poll At a time when many commercial real estate developers are hesitant to break ground on new office buildings, Craig Hall is doing just that. The entrepreneur and founder of HALL Group is moving forward with the next phase of HALL Park, his 162-acre development in Frisco, with a new Class A office tower, an expansion of the popular Kaleidoscope Park, and additional residential development. The investment comes as HALL Park is experiencing renewed leasing momentum, including a major commitment from JPMorganChase and the recent relocation of Public Storage's corporate headquarters from California to HALL Park. For Hall, who began developing HALL Park more than three decades ago, the activity represents another milestone in a much larger vision: transforming what began as a suburban office campus into a thriving mixed-use district where people can work, live, dine, and spend time outside the office. And while the broader office market continues to face questions about demand, construction costs, and the future of the workplace, HALL Group is positioning itself for what it believes will be the next cycle of growth. A Different Kind of Office Market The commercial office market has experienced a fundamental shift in recent years. Remote and hybrid work have changed how companies use their space, while higher construction costs and interest rates have made new development increasingly difficult to justify. But the slowdown in construction may be creating an opportunity for developers willing to take a longer-term view. Across North Texas, relatively few new speculative office buildings are moving forward. At the same time, companies seeking modern, high-quality workplaces are increasingly looking for environments that offer more than traditional office space. HALL Group is betting that this combination of limited future supply and continued demand for premium workplaces will create favorable conditions for its next generation of development. The company's confidence is supported by leasing activity at HALL Park, where several major corporations have recently committed to space. In August, JPMorganChase announced plans to lease approximately 41,000 square feet at The Tower HALL Park, bringing 120 bankers from its commercial banking, private banking, and wealth management divisions to Frisco. The company plans to occupy the space in early 2028, establishing a prominent presence in the 16-story office tower. The recent activity builds on an established corporate tenant base that includes companies such as Public Storage, Deloitte, and Altair Global, reinforcing HALL Park's appeal to both national corporations and growing businesses seeking a presence in North Texas. The commitments are particularly significant given the challenges facing the broader office sector. They suggest that while companies may be reconsidering how much office space they need, demand remains for well-located, highly amenitized buildings that can help attract employees and serve clients. For HALL Group, the leasing momentum also provides a foundation for its next major investment. Building When Others Aren't Construction is underway on The Terraces HALL Park, a 10-story office tower that will bring more than 200,000 square feet of new Class A space to the development. Designed and constructed by The Beck Group, the building represents HALL Group's latest approach to the evolving workplace, emphasizing flexibility, hospitality, and outdoor access. Private terraces will extend from every floor, while a dedicated amenity level will feature meeting spaces, a lounge and bar, and an expansive outdoor terrace overlooking Kaleidoscope Park. Perhaps more notable is how the building's office space will be delivered. Approximately 60% of The Terraces will consist of fully finished, move-in-ready suites, catering to small and midsized companies seeking high-quality space without the time and expense of designing and constructing their own offices. The remaining space will offer customizable options for larger tenants. The strategy reflects a shift in corporate real estate preferences. Rather than committing to large, unfinished spaces and lengthy buildouts, many businesses are prioritizing flexibility, convenience, and workplaces that are ready for immediate use. For developers, it also represents a different approach to attracting tenants in a competitive market. The Terraces is expected to be completed in 2028, arriving at a time when limited new construction could leave companies with fewer options for newly built, premium office space. HALL Group is already considering additional office development as part of its long-term masterplan. From Office Campus to Mixed-Use District While office development remains central to HALL Park's identity, its evolution over the past several years has been equally focused on what happens outside the workplace. The development, which began in the mid-1990s as a collection of office buildings surrounded by landscaped grounds and public art, has expanded into a mixed-use destination with residential towers, a boutique hotel, restaurants, and a major public park. Recent additions include The Monarch at HALL Park, a 214-unit luxury residential tower; HALL Park Hotel, a 224-room Marriott Autograph Collection property; and Kaleidoscope Park, a 5.7-acre public programmed park that opened in October 2024. Together, these developments have changed the experience of HALL Park, bringing activity to the property beyond traditional business hours and creating an environment that serves office tenants, residents, and visitors. The next phase will build on that foundation. HALL Group recently announced Terra Residences, a new 105-home apartment development that will offer studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom floor plans.
